title: OSPF Version 2
summary: Documents version 2 of OSPF, a link-state routing protocol. Routers using it share information about their links so each can compute paths. It was a standards-track document and was replaced by RFC 1583.

eli5.summary: Each router tells all the others what roads it connects to, so every router can draw the same map. This is an early version of those rules.

questions: what is a designated router in ospf
what is the difference between ospf version 1 and version 2
subtitle: The original OSPF version 2 specification: routers share what links they have, then each one computes its own shortest paths.

tldr.problem: Large networks need a routing protocol that reacts quickly to failures, uses little routing traffic, understands IP subnets and Type of Service, and only accepts routing data from trusted routers.
tldr.mechanism: Every OSPF router floods descriptions of its own links to the whole area, so all routers hold an identical database. Each router then runs a shortest-path calculation with itself as the root to build its routing table. Areas, a backbone and a Designated Router on each shared network keep the traffic and database size down.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1247 is a standards-track specification that obsoletes the version 1 spec in RFC 1131. It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 1583 and updated by RFC 1349, so it is of historical interest today.

today: RFC 1247 is obsoleted by RFC 1583 and updated by RFC 1349; it was a Draft Standard that itself obsoleted RFC 1131. It is therefore the early form of OSPF version 2, and later specifications should be consulted for the current protocol.

sections.title: What OSPF Is
sections.content:
RFC 1247 specifies OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) version 2. OSPF is an Internal Gateway Protocol: it distributes routing information between routers that all belong to a single Autonomous System. It was developed by the OSPF working group of the Internet Engineering Task Force.

It is a link-state protocol, which the RFC calls a departure from the Bellman-Ford base used by traditional internet routing protocols. Each router keeps a database describing the topology of the whole Autonomous System, every router holds an identical copy, and every router runs the same algorithm in parallel to compute a tree of shortest paths with itself as the root.

The design is aimed at the internet environment. The RFC lists explicit support for IP subnetting, routing by IP Type of Service (TOS), tagging of externally derived routes, authentication of routing updates, use of IP multicast, equal-cost multipath, and quick recovery from topology changes with a minimum of routing traffic. OSPF routes packets by destination address and TOS only, and the packets are not wrapped in any extra routing header while crossing the Autonomous System.
sections.eli5: Each router tells everyone what it is connected to. Then every router uses the same map to find its own best roads.

sections.title: The Topological Database
sections.content:
The database describes a directed graph. Its vertices are routers, transit networks and stub networks; routers and transit networks can carry traffic that is neither from nor to the router itself, while stub networks cannot. An edge joins two routers connected by a point-to-point network, and an edge from a router to a network means the router has an interface on that network.

OSPF distinguishes three kinds of physical network: point-to-point networks, broadcast networks (many routers plus the ability to address all of them at once, such as an ethernet) and non-broadcast networks (many routers but no broadcast, such as an X.25 public data network). Neighbors are found dynamically on broadcast networks, while non-broadcast networks need some configuration.

A configurable cost is attached to the output side of each router interface; the lower the cost, the more likely the interface is used. Each router builds a shortest-path tree from this graph. Only the next hop of each route is used for forwarding. When several equal-cost routes exist, they are all discovered and traffic is shared among them.

OSPF can also compute a separate set of routes for each IP Type of Service. A cost for TOS 0 must always be configured. An implementation must be able to route by TOS, but a router can be configured to use only TOS 0 to save table space and processing, and such routers are avoided as much as possible for non-zero TOS traffic.
sections.eli5: The map shows places and the roads between them, and each road has a price tag. The cheaper the road, the more likely you are to use it.

sections.title: Areas, the Backbone and Router Roles
sections.content:
An Autonomous System can be split into areas: groups of contiguous networks and hosts, plus the routers attached to them. Each area runs its own copy of the basic algorithm and has its own database, and its topology is hidden from the rest of the system. This cuts routing traffic and protects intra-area routing from bad routing data coming from outside the area.

Areas are tied together by the backbone, which must be contiguous. If the areas leave it disconnected, the administrator restores connectivity with virtual links, which are treated as unnumbered point-to-point networks that belong to the backbone. Traffic between two areas crosses the backbone in three pieces: an intra-area path to an area border router, a backbone path, and an intra-area path to the destination.

Routers fall into four overlapping classes. Internal routers have all interfaces in one area. Area border routers attach to several areas, run one copy of the algorithm per area, and summarize each area for the backbone. Backbone routers have an interface to the backbone. AS boundary routers exchange routing information with other Autonomous Systems.

Each area is defined as a list of address ranges, written as address and mask pairs. An area border router advertises one route per range, at the minimum cost of any network in the range. An area can also be configured as a stub area: AS external advertisements are not flooded into it and the area uses a default route advertised by its area border routers. Virtual links cannot pass through stub areas and AS boundary routers cannot be inside them.

The RFC says OSPF does not actively repair area partitions. A partitioned area simply becomes separate areas that the backbone routes between, but the backbone itself must not partition.
sections.eli5: A big town is split into neighborhoods. Each neighborhood knows its own streets well, and a main road joins them all, so nobody has to remember every street in town.

sections.title: External Routes and Subnets
sections.content:
Routes learned from outside the Autonomous System, for example from EGP, or configured statically, are flooded unaltered by AS boundary routers and kept separate from OSPF's own link state data. They are examined after the shortest-path tree is built and appear on it as leaves.

Two kinds of external metric exist. A Type 1 metric is equivalent to the link state metric, so the total is the external cost plus the distance to the advertising router. A Type 2 metric is larger than any internal path cost, so the boundary router with the smallest external metric wins no matter how far away it is, and the internal distance is used only to break ties. If both types are present, Type 1 takes precedence.

An external advertisement can carry a forwarding address so that packets go straight to the real next router instead of making an extra hop through the AS boundary router. The same field lets an interior router act as a route server.

Every advertised route carries an IP address mask, which allows variable length subnets. A packet is forwarded using the best match, meaning the longest or most specific one, and host routes use the mask 0xffffffff.
sections.eli5: Roads that lead outside the town are posted with a price too. You either add that price to your trip, or you just pick the exit with the cheapest sign.

sections.title: Neighbors, Adjacencies and the Designated Router
sections.content:
The Hello protocol finds neighbors and checks that communication works in both directions: a router knows it is bidirectional when it sees itself listed in a neighbor's Hello packet. Hellos are sent on every interface; on broadcast and point-to-point networks they go to the multicast address AllSPFRouters. Routers on one network must agree on the network mask and on the hello and dead intervals, and a mismatch stops the neighbor relationship forming.

Not every pair of neighbors becomes adjacent. Adjacent routers synchronize their databases through a Database Exchange: they pick a master and a slave, the master polls with numbered Database Description packets, and the slave answers by echoing the sequence number. The M-bit signals more packets to follow. Each side then requests newer advertisements with Link State Request packets. When all requests are satisfied, the routers are fully adjacent and the adjacency appears in their advertisements.

Every multi-access network has a Designated Router. It originates the network links advertisement and becomes adjacent to all other routers on the network, which keeps the number of adjacencies and the routing traffic down. A Backup Designated Router is also adjacent to all, and takes over without any new database synchronization when the Designated Router fails. Both are elected by the Hello protocol using Router Priority, with the highest Router ID breaking ties. A priority of 0 makes a router ineligible. A router that finds a Designated Router already present accepts it, so the role changes as rarely as possible.
sections.eli5: Routers first wave hello to each other. Then neighbors that want to trade notes compare what they know. On a crowded street, one chosen router collects everyone's notes so nobody has to talk to everybody.

sections.title: OSPF Packets
sections.content:
OSPF runs directly over IP, as IP protocol number 89, with no fragmentation of its own; it relies on IP fragmentation and recommends avoiding it by splitting large exchanges into several smaller packets. Routing packets are sent with IP TOS 0 and with IP precedence set to Internetwork Control. Multicast packets use TTL 1, and the two multicast addresses are AllSPFRouters (224.0.0.5) and AllDRouters (224.0.0.6).

Every packet starts with a common 24 byte header carrying the version (2), packet type, length, Router ID, Area ID, a checksum, an authentication type and a 64-bit authentication field. There are five packet types. Hello packets discover and maintain neighbors; Database Description and Link State Request packets bring up adjacencies; Link State Update and Link State Acknowledgment packets make flooding reliable.

Packets also carry an options field with two defined bits. The E-bit shows whether a router handles AS external advertisements, and two routers will not become neighbors unless they agree on it, which keeps stub area configuration consistent. The T-bit shows TOS capability. Receivers ignore unrecognized capabilities.
sections.eli5: Every OSPF message starts with the same little label saying who sent it, which neighborhood it is for and what kind of message it is.

sections.title: Advertisements, Flooding and Route Calculation
sections.content:
The database is made of link state advertisements, each with a 20-byte header. The LS type, Link State ID and Advertising Router identify an advertisement, and the sequence number, checksum and age decide which of two instances is newer. The sequence number is a signed 32-bit integer; the checksum is the Fletcher checksum that covers everything except the age. An age is never allowed to exceed MaxAge, which is 1 hour, and an advertisement is reoriginated at least every LSRefreshTime of 30 minutes.

There are five advertisement types: router links, network links, two kinds of summary links (to networks and to AS boundary routers) and AS external links. All except AS external links stay inside one area.

Flooding is reliable. A router sends a new advertisement out its eligible interfaces in Link State Update packets and keeps it on a retransmission list for each neighbor until it is acknowledged, either by a Link State Acknowledgment packet or by receiving the same advertisement back. On broadcast networks the Designated Router and Backup multicast to AllSPFRouters, while other routers use AllDRouters. A router that receives an old copy of its own advertisement after a restart must raise the sequence number past it.

The routing table is computed in stages. First, Dijkstra's algorithm builds the shortest-path tree over routers and transit networks, using a link only if both ends advertise it, and then stub networks are added as leaves. Next come inter-area routes from summary advertisements, resolution of virtual link next hops, and finally the external routes. Each non-zero TOS is calculated separately.
sections.eli5: When a router learns something new, it tells its neighbors and keeps asking until they say thanks. Once the news has spread, every router redraws its own shortest-path map.

sections.title: Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC states that all OSPF exchanges are authenticated, using the authentication type and the 64-bit authentication field in the packet header. The authentication type is configured per area and the key per interface, so different areas can use stricter schemes than others.

Only two types are defined. Type 0 means no authentication and the field is not examined. Type 1 is a simple password: a clear 64-bit value configured per network and placed in every packet. The RFC says this guards against routers coming up in an area by accident, since they must be given the network's password first. All other types are reserved for assignment by the IANA.
sections.eli5: Routers can use a secret word before they are allowed to join the conversation. The simple version is just a password everyone says out loud.

sections.title: Changes From Version 1
sections.content:
Appendix F lists the differences from OSPF version 1 in RFC 1131. The changes are not backward compatible, so version 1 and version 2 will not interoperate.

  • Stub areas let an area ignore AS external advertisements and use a default route instead.
  • Optional TOS support: version 1 required every router to route by TOS. In version 2 a router can use only TOS 0 and say so with the T-bit.
  • Forwarding address: a new field in AS external advertisements prevents extra hops to external destinations.

The appendix also describes corrected problems and packet format changes. The options field is meant to let future additions be made in a backward-compatible way.
sections.eli5: Version 2 fixed some things from version 1, but it speaks a bit differently, so the old and new versions cannot talk to each other.
